requirements.text: std/json gives read access to a parsed document (owned accessors, cursors, dotted paths, index chains) and typed decode errors; the children below say what each group returns.

jsonParse accepts a string if and only if it is a JSON text as defined by RFC 8259 (subject to the stated implementation limits JSON-DEPTH, JSON-NUM-RANGE and JSON-BOM), and returns Err for every other string.
Every serializer in std/json (jsonSer, the builders, jsonEscapeStr, jsonPretty) produces valid RFC 8259 JSON text, and parsing that text gives back the value that was serialized.
jsoncParse accepts RFC 8259 JSON plus comments and trailing commas, and nothing else.
jsonPull is a streaming tokenizer: it yields the tokens of a JSON text one at a time without building a tree.
On any input, however malformed or large, the parser and the tokenizer terminate, read only inside the input, and compute no overflowing integer; the worst outcome is Err or an Error token.
RFC 8259 s2: a JSON text is optional whitespace, one value, optional whitespace; any value type is allowed at the top level. Empty or whitespace-only input and any content after the value are errors.

RFC 8259 s2: the only whitespace is space, horizontal tab, line feed and carriage return, between tokens. Any other character (vertical tab, form feed, no-break space, U+2028, NUL) outside a string is an error.
RFC 8259 s3: the literals are exactly the lower-case names true, false and null. A prefix, a different case or a longer name is an error.

RFC 8259 s4: an object is { } or { member *( , member ) } with member = string : value. Unquoted or non-string names, a missing colon or value, a missing, doubled or trailing comma and an unclosed or mismatched bracket are errors.

RFC 8259 s4 (names SHOULD be unique): duplicate names are not an error. The parser keeps every member in source order; a lookup by name (get, str, i64, f64, bool, curField) returns the first member with that name.
RFC 8259 s5: an array is [ ] or [ value *( , value ) ]. A missing, doubled or trailing comma, a colon in place of a comma and an unclosed or mismatched bracket are errors.

RFC 8259 s6: number = [ - ] int [ . 1*digit ] [ (e|E) [ + | - ] 1*digit ], int = 0 / (1-9 *digit). Leading zeros, a leading plus, a leading or trailing decimal point, an exponent with no digits, hex, octal, Infinity and NaN are errors.

RFC 8259 s6 (implementations may limit range and precision): a number of any length is accepted. Its f64 value is the correctly rounded strtod value, +/-infinity past the f64 range and 0 below it. The integer accessors answer Some only for an integer literal that fits i64 (u64 for curUint) and None otherwise, never a truncation. rawStr returns the literal verbatim.

RFC 8259 s7: a string is delimited by double quotes and holds any character except the quote, the backslash and the control characters U+0000 to U+001F, which must be escaped. An unterminated string, a raw control character (including tab and line feed) and single quotes are errors.
RFC 8259 s7: the escapes are \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX, each decoding to its character. Any other escape letter, a lone backslash at the end and a backslash-newline are errors.
RFC 8259 s7: \u is followed by exactly four hexadecimal digits, upper or lower case. Fewer digits or a non-hex digit are errors.

RFC 8259 s7: an escaped UTF-16 surrogate pair (\uD83D\uDE00) decodes to one code point and is stored as its 4-byte UTF-8 form. RFC 8259 s8.2 leaves a lone surrogate escape unpredictable; this parser accepts it and decodes it to U+FFFD, so a decoded string is always valid UTF-8.

RFC 8259 s8.1: JSON text is UTF-8. A byte at or above 0x80 inside a string must begin a well-formed UTF-8 sequence (RFC 3629: no overlong form, no surrogate, nothing above U+10FFFF); ill-formed UTF-8 (Latin-1, truncated or lone continuation bytes, 5- and 6-byte forms, encoded surrogates) is an error. Non-ASCII bytes outside a string are errors by JSON-WS.

RFC 8259 s8.1 (a parser MAY ignore a leading byte order mark rather than treat it as an error): this parser does not ignore it; a leading UTF-8 BOM is an error. UTF-16 and UTF-32 text is not UTF-8 and is an error.
RFC 8259 s9 (a parser may limit nesting depth): nesting up to JSON_MAX_DEPTH (512) containers is accepted; deeper input is an Err naming the depth limit, never a stack overflow.

RFC 8259 s7: jsonEscapeStr escapes the quote and the backslash, writes the control characters U+0000 to U+001F as \n, \t, \r or \u00xx, and copies every other byte unchanged, so valid UTF-8 stays valid UTF-8.
RFC 8259 s4, s5: jsonSer and the object and array builders emit commas only between members, quote and escape every name, and close every container, so their output is accepted by jsonParse.
RFC 8259 s6: an integer serializes as its decimal digits and a finite float as a JSON number; NaN and the infinities, which JSON cannot express, serialize as null.

Parsing the serializer's output gives back the value serialized: strings (every byte string that is valid UTF-8, control characters included), integers, finite floats, booleans, null, array order and object member order.
jsonPretty changes only the whitespace between tokens: its output is valid JSON, parses to the same value, and keeps every string and number literal byte for byte.
// to end of line and /* */ comments outside a string count as whitespace (a comment between two digits does not join them); the same characters inside a string are text.
One trailing comma after the last element of an array or the last member of an object is accepted. A comma with no value before it ([,] , [1,,] , {,}) is still an error.
Apart from comments and trailing commas, jsoncParse applies jsonParse's rules unchanged: every other malformed input is an Err.

For a valid JSON text jsonPull yields StartObject, EndObject, StartArray, EndArray, Key, Str, Num, Bool and Null tokens in document order (a string in an object name position is a Key, elsewhere a Str; Num carries the f64 value jsonParse would give), then End, with string text decoded like jsonParse.

A token that is malformed on its own (a misspelled literal, a number against JSON-NUM-GRAMMAR, a string against JSON-STR-CHARS, JSON-STR-ESC, JSON-STR-UESC or JSON-UTF8) yields an Error token; Error is final.
Known limit: jsonPull does not check structure (bracket matching, commas, colons, one root value); it is a tokenizer. A caller that needs validation parses with jsonParse.

The owned accessors (get, str, i64, f64, bool, at, asStr, asI64, asF64, asBool, isNull, isStr, isNum, isBool, isArray, isObject, len, keys, rawStr) answer Some or the value only when the node has the asked-for kind or key: None for a missing key, an out-of-range or negative index, a wrong kind or a non-container, never a coerced value. get and at return the subtree as a document of its own whose rawStr is the subtree's source text.

A dotted path ("a.b", "items[0].name") resolves one member or element per step; path, strPath, i64Path, f64Path, boolPath, curPath, curAt and the *At readers return None (cursor -1) for a missing key, an out-of-range index, a step into a scalar, a non-digit inside brackets or an unterminated bracket, and otherwise the same value the step-by-step accessors give.

Cursor navigation (curRoot, curChild, curField, curLen, curKind, curHolds, curKeyAt, curValueAt, curItems and the cur* readers) allocates no tree and reports a miss as cursor -1, which every reader treats as nothing here (length 0, kind -1, None, empty text); it answers exactly as the owned accessors do. A cursor minted by one document is not held by another.

The index chain (idxRoot, idxKey, idxPos, idxPath and the idx* readers behind doc["a"][0]) answers exactly as the cursor API it wraps; a step that finds nothing yields a position where idxExists is false and every read is absent.

A JsonError names where decoding failed: path() is the dotted location (indices abut as [3], a syntax error has none), under and underIndex prefix one segment, message() states the field, the expected kind and the found kind, and jsonKindName maps a cursor kind to its name (-1 is missing).

The fluent builders (Json.obj and Json.arr, jsonObj, jsonArr, every typed method, the *Opt forms, raw, val, spread, build and buildPretty) append members and elements in call order, an *Opt method adds its key only for Some, and the built text parses back to the same members, in order, with the same kinds and values; after spread a repeated key replaces its value in place.

Derived requirement (the flat node pool is an implementation choice the system level did not ask for): a parsed node stores its kind and payload without loss, so after parsing, kind, boolean value, number, string text, child count and child order read back exactly what the source holds, and a handed-over pool serves the same document.
Every scanning helper (jsonUtf8SeqLen, jsonScanString, jsonScanNumber, jsonLitAt, jsonSkipWs, the integer readers) reads only indices inside the string it scans and never moves its cursor backward.
The integer readers jsonNodeInt and jsonNodeUint never overflow while accumulating digits: a literal past the type's range answers None.
